\chapter{Numbers Eleven to Twenty}
\label{ch:ar-numbers-eleven-to-twenty}
\hlchaptermodality{20}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from eleven to twenty in Arabic and build the teens as 'X and ten'.}

Build the teens as additive X-ʿashar compounds, then say ʿishrūn, which is not built that way at all.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{أحد} \ar{عشر} — \ar{عشرون}]{\ar{أحد} \ar{عشر}, \ar{عشرون} — plain compounds, then a genuinely different twenty}

\label{lesson:AR-C20-ahada-ashar-ishrun}



\begin{quote}
Eleven through fifteen build the same simple way every time. Then twenty breaks the pattern completely — it isn't built the way you'd expect at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{أحد} \ar{عشر} – \ar{خمسة} \ar{عشر} — \textquotedblleft{}X and ten\textquotedblright{}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{أحد} \ar{عشر}} & \emph{aḥada ʿashar} — \textquotedblleft{}one-ten\textquotedblright{} (11) \\
\textbf{\ar{اثنا} \ar{عشر}} & \emph{ithnā ʿashar} — \textquotedblleft{}two-ten\textquotedblright{} (12) \\
\textbf{\ar{ثلاثة} \ar{عشر}} & \emph{thalāthata ʿashar} — \textquotedblleft{}three-ten\textquotedblright{} (13) \\
\textbf{\ar{أربعة} \ar{عشر}} & \emph{arbaʿata ʿashar} — \textquotedblleft{}four-ten\textquotedblright{} (14) \\
\textbf{\ar{خمسة} \ar{عشر}} & \emph{khamsata ʿashar} — \textquotedblleft{}five-ten\textquotedblright{} (15) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every one of these is the counting-word (from the AGE and NUM-1-5 lessons) plus \textbf{\ar{عشر}} (\emph{ʿashar}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ten}\textquotedblright{}) — a straightforward additive compound, the same shape Spanish builds in \emph{once}-\emph{quince} and Latin in \emph{ūndecim}-\emph{quīndecim}.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{عشرون} — NOT \textquotedblleft{}two-ten,\textquotedblright{} a genuinely different word}
Here's the honest surprise: \textbf{twenty} is \textbf{not} built from \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} + \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} the way 11-15 were built. \textbf{\ar{عشرون}} (\emph{ʿishrūn}, \textquotedblleft{}twenty\textquotedblright{}) is its \textbf{own}, distinct word — a special \textbf{plural-like form} built directly on the same \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} root, \textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{ش}-\ar{ر}} (\emph{ʿ-sh-r}), rather than a compound of \emph{ithnān} (\textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{ʿashar} (\textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}). That root, \emph{ʿashar}/\emph{ʿishrūn}, is the same Semitic \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} root behind Hebrew's \textbf{\he{עֶשֶׂר}} (\emph{eser}, \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}) — and, coincidentally, resembles the Indo-European \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} root that gives English its own \textbf{-teen} suffix, though the two roots are \textbf{not} related: Arabic and English inherited \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} from two entirely separate language families, so this is a parallel, not a shared borrowing or common ancestor.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}aḥada ʿashar, ithnā ʿashar, thalāthata ʿashar\textquotedblright{} — 11, 12, 13, \textquotedblleft{}X and ten\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ʿishrūn\textquotedblright{} — twenty, its OWN word, not \textquotedblleft{}two-ten\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How are 11-15 built in Arabic? (\textbf{X + ʿashar} — \textquotedblleft{}one-ten,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}two-ten,\textquotedblright{} and so on, a plain additive compound.) Is \textbf{\ar{عشرون}} (twenty) built the same way, as \textquotedblleft{}two-ten\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{No} — it's a distinct, standalone plural-like form built on the same \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} root, not a compound of \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}ten.\textquotedblright{}) What root does \textbf{ʿashar}/\textbf{ʿishrūn} share with Hebrew? (\textbf{\he{ע}-\he{ש}-\he{ר}}/\textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{ش}-\ar{ر}}, the Semitic root for \textquotedblleft{}ten,\textquotedblright{} giving Hebrew's \emph{eser}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
